title: The widows' complaint (Acts 6:1–7)
hookLine: Greek-speaking widows are overlooked, so seven are chosen to serve tables
tomorrow: a man with a face like an angel tells his people's story. why?

cards: At a big family party there's often someone on the edge: the aunt who doesn't speak the language well, the grandparent served last. Acts 6 has that.
The community is growing, food is handed out every day, and "there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration." Who notices?
The people being missed, first. They complain. And the apostles listen.

teach.b: Today's question: who makes sure nobody gets missed? The twelve call everyone together and admit their limits: "It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables."
So the community chooses "seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom." The people who will carry plates are asked first for wisdom and the Spirit.
Listen to the names: Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, Nicolas. Some readers notice they're Greek names, from the same side as the widows who were overlooked.
The apostles pray and lay their hands on them. One to tell a friend tonight: Acts never uses the word deacon in this chapter.
The work is diakonia, serving, and some churches read this as the start of that role. Now a neighbor who shares this.

teach.h: THE QUR'AN: FOOD, FOR LOVE OF GOD.
teach.b: The Qur'an describes the righteous as those who feed the needy, the orphan and the prisoner for love of God, saying, in effect: we feed you for God's sake alone; we want no reward from you, and no thanks.
Feeding the overlooked, quietly, for God: Christians and Muslims both hold that close.
One honest difference: Acts answers by setting people apart for the task, with prayer and hands; the Qur'an's verses describe the heart of anyone who feeds, and what they don't ask in return.

how: Churches differ on what a deacon is: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches ordain deacons as clergy, and in some Protestant churches deacons are members chosen to serve the congregation's needs.

o: a senior pastor who leads the services
a church treasurer who manages the money
one set apart to serve others in the church

games.q: at a family reunion, your great-aunt, who speaks little English, sits alone while plates go around. you're busy helping in the kitchen. what fits Acts 6?
o: bring her a plate first, and sit with her a minute.
finish the kitchen work; someone else will notice her.
tell your mom later that the seating plan was unfair.
games.why: the widows were neglected in the daily ministration until people were set apart to serve them. serving tables starts with noticing.

practice: Close your eyes and walk through a room you'll be in this week: a table, a class, a group chat. Look slowly for the person at the edge, the one served last or heard least.
If you pray, you can hold their name; if not, just keep their face in view, and choose one small way to bring them in.

wordCard.voice: Deacon. The serving role some churches trace to Acts 6: people set apart so no widow is missed at the table.

orig.note: Greek: to serve, to wait on; the verb in serve tables, Acts 6:2.

carryVoice: Carry this: serve tables, and look for the name that got skipped. Day eleven of Acts.
